title: SpaceX Finances $40 Billion of Nvidia Chips Like an Aircraft Fleet
subtitle: A master finance lease with an Apollo-managed entity turns five years of GPUs into 20 quarterly payments
summary: SpaceX signed a binding commitment for a roughly $40 billion equipment lease arranged by Apollo to fund next-generation Nvidia chips. The structure pays the hardware off over five years and leans on rocket and broadband cash flow to borrow at terms pure-play AI clouds cannot match.

bodyHtml:
Think about how major commercial airlines build their fleets. They almost never pay cash on the tarmac. Instead, large financial syndicates buy the planes and rent them to the airline over twenty years. SpaceX is now applying that same template to artificial intelligence hardware.

Strip away the orbital launches and SpaceX runs three businesses. It flies rockets for commercial and government customers. It sells Starlink satellite internet to homes, ships and airlines. And its Super Intelligence division rents computing power, builds Grok, and runs Cursor, the coding tool your software friends keep open all day.

Compute is no longer a sideline. Super Intelligence became the company's largest business in the September quarter. It generated $7.56 billion of the $14.58 billion total and posted $431 million of operating profit, after losing $1.26 billion the quarter before. To keep building, SpaceX signed a binding commitment on Oct. 24 for a roughly $40 billion lease managed by Apollo Global Management.

The mechanics matter, because this is not a bond. An entity managed by Apollo buys the GPU pods and related equipment outright and leases them to SpaceX, which picks the data centers but never owns the chips. The hardware lands in tranches, each running about five to five and a quarter years.

Rent is paid quarterly in advance at one-twentieth of the financed cost of each tranche, plus a fixed rate on the outstanding balance. Twenty equal principal payments means SpaceX retires 100% of the purchase price over the lease. It looks like a phone payment plan scaled up to institutional finance, and Apollo is not betting on what a used accelerator fetches in 2031.

SpaceX has run this play before. Filings show a subsidiary booked three similar sale-leaseback financings with Valor Equity Partners for compute hardware. They are carried as $12.9 billion of debt with $351 million of interest expense last quarter. Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen said the new lease diversifies funding sources and covers a notable chunk of what the growth plan requires.

What makes the borrowing cheap is the rest of the company. All three major agencies rated SpaceX investment grade in June, with stable outlooks: Moody's at Baa1, Fitch at BBB+, S&P at BBB. The gap this creates is enormous. CoreWeave's 2031 bonds yielded about 15.8% this month, with credit default swaps near 1,038 basis points. Lambda borrowed at 6.78% because two investment-grade customers stood behind the paper. Same industry, same silicon, a nine-point spread, because rockets and satellite dishes pay the baseline bills.

Megaleases are becoming the machinery of the boom. Apollo and Blackstone arranged about $35 billion of chip leasing for Anthropic, Meta wrapped a $27 billion joint venture around its Louisiana campus, and Oracle's build for OpenAI lined up $38 billion. Nobody funds the whole bill from the register anymore.

Here is the tension. SpaceX is pairing a fixed five-year obligation with revenue it keeps deliberately loose. Musk said on the earnings call that SpaceX rents compute at effectively the spot market rate rather than signing long-term customer deals. Capacity splits roughly half internal, half third party. Management adds that compute pricing is running slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range it laid out last quarter, and claims payback periods under one year.

For the equity, that reframes the question. It is no longer whether SpaceX can buy compute, since the answer is yes. It is whether the silicon throws off cash faster than the payment schedule and the depreciation schedule catch up. Growth multiples in the high fifties to low sixties leave little tolerance for a payback estimate that slips.

The bear case says the lease is debt wearing a costume. Twenty payments of principal repay the full purchase price, so the only differences from a bond are the label and the collateral. Add it to the $39 billion of debt and finance leases already on the books and pro forma leverage lands near $79 billion. On top of that sit $37.8 billion of non-cancelable commitments, with $25.6 billion due next year.

The residual value risk sits with SpaceX, not Apollo, because a full-payout lease leaves the lessor whole. SpaceX needs five years of economic life from hardware Nvidia refreshes annually, while the revenue underneath is repriced in the spot market. Musk himself warned that debt markets have largely shut out companies without cash flow outside data centers. He predicted more than 200 neoclouds face what he called guppy-level death and consolidation. If rental rates reset lower, SpaceX's third-party half catches the same price. Cash and cash equivalents fell from $93.5 billion to $51.3 billion in one quarter, though most of that was a shift into short-term marketable securities, leaving total liquidity down about $10 billion at $89.9 billion. December-quarter capex alone is guided at $35 billion to $40 billion.

What resolves it is the part nobody can see yet. The fixed rate on the Apollo schedules gets priced before signing. The first tranches will therefore reveal exactly how much of that investment-grade rating SpaceX gets to keep. Deliveries start in the first half of 2027. Watch that number the way you would watch a mortgage rate on a house you already agreed to buy.

SpaceX is betting that satellite cash flow can permanently subsidize the cost of intelligence. Wall Street is happy to own the hardware and collect the rent. Now the chips have to pay their own freight down on Earth.
